\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:ar-family}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my father, mother, brother and sister in Arabic.}

Say akh and ukht, show how ukht is built from the same root plus a feminine -t, and place both beside their Hebrew cousins.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{أب} \ar{أم}]{\ar{أب}, \ar{أم} (ab, umm) — father and mother}

\label{lesson:AR-C10-ab-umm}



\begin{quote}
Two short, ancient words — each just two or three letters — sitting at the root of Semitic family vocabulary across several languages, not just Arabic.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أب}} (\emph{ab}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father}.\textquotedblright{} A short, ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אב}} (\emph{av}) and Aramaic \textbf{\he{אבא}} (\emph{abba}) — the very word behind \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Abba, Father}\textquotedblright{} in the New Testament.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أم}} (\emph{umm}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother}.\textquotedblright{} Equally ancient, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אם}} (\emph{em}).
\end{itemize}

These aren't borrowings between Arabic and Hebrew — both descend from the same ancient Semitic family vocabulary, the way \emph{pater} and English \emph{father} are cousins through PIE rather than one copying the other.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{أم}} stays productive in everyday Arabic naming: \textbf{\ar{أم}} + a child's name forms a \textbf{kunya}, an honorific \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother of \_\_\_}\textquotedblright{} (and \textbf{\ar{أبو}}, \emph{abū}, does the same for fathers — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father of \_\_\_}\textquotedblright{}). Someone might be known publicly as \emph{Umm Khālid}, \textquotedblleft{}mother of Khālid,\textquotedblright{} rather than by their own given name — a naming custom still very much alive today.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ab\textquotedblright{} — father — then \textquotedblleft{}umm,\textquotedblright{} mother
  \item the Hebrew cousins — \textquotedblleft{}ab/av, umm/em\textquotedblright{}
  \item the naming pattern — \textquotedblleft{}Umm + {[}child's name{]}\textquotedblright{} = mother of \_\_\_
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are Arabic's words for father and mother? (\textbf{\ar{أب} ab, \ar{أم} umm}.) What are their Hebrew cousins? (\textbf{av, em} — not borrowings, both from the same ancient Semitic root.) What naming pattern does \textbf{umm} still form today? (\textbf{Umm + {[}child's name{]}}, \textquotedblleft{}mother of \_\_\_,\textquotedblright{} a living honorific.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{أخ} \ar{أخت}]{\ar{أخ}, \ar{أخت} (akh, ukht) — brother and sister}

\label{lesson:AR-C10-akh-ukht}



\begin{quote}
Unlike the color words you just learned (a whole reshaped template for masculine/feminine), siblings here use the \textbf{simplest} possible gender marker.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أخ}} (\emph{akh}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{brother}\textquotedblright{} — another short, ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אח}} (\emph{ach}).
  \item \textbf{\ar{أخت}} (\emph{ukht}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sister}\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{same root}, plus a plain feminine \textbf{‑\ar{ت}} (\emph{‑t}) ending, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{אחות}} (\emph{achot}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{ukht} isn't a separate word — it's \emph{akh} wearing the ordinary feminine ending, the simple pattern you already know from \textbf{\ar{آسف}/\ar{آسفة}} (\emph{āsif/āsifa}, \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}), not the elaborate colors template.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akh\textquotedblright{} — brother — then \textquotedblleft{}ukht,\textquotedblright{} sister
  \item the shared root plus a simple ending — akh + ‑t
  \item the Hebrew cousins — \textquotedblleft{}akh/ach, ukht/achot\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are Arabic's words for brother and sister? (\textbf{\ar{أخ} akh, \ar{أخت} ukht}.) How is \emph{ukht} built from \emph{akh}? (\textbf{The same root, plus a plain feminine ‑\ar{ت} ending} — the simple pattern, not the colors' elaborate template.) What are their Hebrew cousins? (\textbf{ach, achot}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mā ismuka? · ismī …]{The name exchange, cold}

\label{lesson:AR-R10-the-name-exchange-cold}



\begin{quote}
Eight lessons ago this book taught you to give your name and ask for somebody else's, and has not asked since. Say the whole exchange from memory before you read another line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{letters, right to left} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{اسم}} \emph{ism} & \emph{alif · sīn · mīm} & name — root \textbf{s–m–w}, cousin of Hebrew \emph{shem} \\
\textbf{\ar{ما}} \emph{mā} & \emph{mīm · alif} & what, standing before a noun \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neither needed a new letter. \textbf{\ar{اسم}} has no tie to English \emph{name} or Latin \emph{nōmen} — the resemblance is an accident, and the real cousin is Hebrew.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four suffixes and no verb}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{glued on} & \textbf{means} & \textbf{gives} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{ـي}} \emph{-ī} & my & \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} \emph{ismī} \\
\textbf{\ar{ـك}} \emph{-ka} & your, to a man & \textbf{\ar{اسمك}} \emph{ismuka} \\
\textbf{\ar{ـك}} \emph{-ki} & your, to a woman & \textbf{\ar{اسمك}} \emph{ismuki} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Arabic has no separate word for \emph{my}. It fastens \textbf{\ar{ي}}, the \emph{yāʾ}, onto the end of the noun — the habit that also fastens \textbf{\ar{الـ}} for \emph{the}. The suffixes are the grammar of the exchange, and the two written forms of \emph{your name} are identical on the page.

There is no word for \textbf{is} either. \emph{Ismī Arun} is literally \emph{my-name Arun} — the zero copula, shared with the Dravidian languages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The two words: \ar{أنت}, split by the listener}
\textbf{\ar{أنت}} is \emph{alif} with a hamza seat, then \emph{nūn}, then \emph{tāʾ} — one skeleton for both genders. What splits them is a vowel mark that everyday text leaves off: \textbf{\ar{أنتَ}} \emph{anta} to a man, \textbf{\ar{أنتِ}} \emph{anti} to a woman.

The European and Dravidian tracks split \emph{you} by \textbf{register}. Arabic splits it by the \textbf{listener's gender} instead — and the Semitic \emph{-ta} / \emph{-ti} ending is the same \emph{t} that marks \emph{you} in Hebrew \emph{atta} / \emph{att}.

\subsection*{The exchange}
\textbf{\ar{تشرفنا}} \emph{tasharrafnā} closes it — letters \emph{tāʾ · shīn · rāʾ · fāʾ}, root \textbf{sh–r–f}, honour: \emph{sharaf} (honour), \emph{sharīf} (noble, the title behind English \emph{sheriff}). The polite close is not \emph{pleased to meet you} but \textbf{we have been honoured}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a man for his name — \emph{mā ismuka?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a woman — \emph{mā ismuki?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} answer with your own — \emph{ismī …}
  \item \emph{Say it:} close the exchange — \emph{tasharrafnā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the verb Arabic left out of every line above
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the Hebrew cousin of \textbf{\ar{اسم}}. (\emph{Shem}.) Say which axis Arabic uses to split \textbf{\ar{أنت}}, where register would be the obvious choice. (\textbf{The listener's gender}.) Give the literal sense of \textbf{\ar{تشرفنا}}. (\emph{\textbf{We have been honoured}}.) And say where the gender of the question sits. (\textbf{In the suffix} — \emph{-ka} to a man, \emph{-ki} to a woman.)
\end{tcolorbox}
